steps.title: Plays with names
steps.body: A few plays are so famous they ==have their own names==. Fans still bring them up decades later, usually to annoy the other team's fans.

steps.title: The Immaculate Reception
steps.body: 1972, Pittsburgh down late in a playoff game. A pass ==deflects off a collision== and Franco Harris ==scoops it just before it hits the ground==, then runs it in to win.

steps.title: The Catch
steps.body: 1982, San Francisco. Joe Montana rolls right under pressure and lofts it high. Dwight Clark ==leaps at the back of the end zone== to win the game and start a dynasty.

steps.title: The Hail Mary
steps.body: In a 1975 playoff game, Dallas QB Roger Staubach heaved a ==long, desperate pass== for the winning score, then said he'd thrown it and said a Hail Mary. Every ==last-second heave== has had the name since.

steps.title: The Helmet Catch
steps.body: In the 2008 title game, Eli Manning escaped a sack and threw deep. David Tyree ==pinned the ball to his helmet== with one hand, and New York ==ended New England's perfect season==.

steps.title: The perfect season
steps.body: The 1972 Miami team went ==17–0==, still the ==only perfect season== in pro football. Some of its players famously toast each year when the last unbeaten team loses.

steps.prompt: Four seconds left, 50 yards to go. What's this play called?
steps.explain: A long, high, last-second throw into a crowded end zone is a Hail Mary, named after Roger Staubach's 1975 prayer.

steps.prompt: What made the Immaculate Reception famous?
options: A receiver caught it with one hand on his helmet
A deflected pass was caught just before it hit the ground
It was the longest field goal ever kicked
The quarterback guaranteed the win beforehand
steps.explain: The pass bounced off a collision and Franco Harris grabbed it near his shoetops, then ran for the winning touchdown.
